stories.headline: 800,000 Front Range voters received ballots with erroneous passenger rail tax question
stories.summary:
An estimated 800,000 voters in Adams, Arapahoe, Douglas and Weld counties received ballots incorrectly including Ballot Issue 7A, a proposed sales tax increase to fund the Colorado Connector passenger rail line connecting Pueblo to Fort Collins. The error occurred because the Front Range Passenger Rail District failed to provide updated boundary maps to county clerks after the Colorado General Assembly narrowed the district's boundaries in May.

The district's general counsel, Brent Butzin, apologized in a letter to county clerks, acknowledging the new boundaries were not shared through the usual channels. Election officials are directing voters to fill out their ballots as normal, with clerks to use precinct maps after the election to determine which votes on Issue 7A are valid and which should be discarded.

Douglas County Clerk and Recorder Sheri Davis said her office had only received a map showing all of Douglas County within the district and used that map to prepare ballots. The Colorado Secretary of State's office is working with the Colorado County Clerks Association to develop guidance for counties on proper administration of the contested ballot issue. Libertarian activist Jon Caldara of the Independence Institute called for the measure to be invalidated entirely.

stories.headline: Avalanche fall to Jets 3-2 in Winnipeg as Colorado drops to 2-1 on season
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche lost 3-2 to the Winnipeg Jets on Wednesday night, with Kyle Connor breaking a tie with a minute remaining by scoring his second goal of the game. Goaltender Stuart Skinner made 32 saves for the Jets, who earned their third straight victory of the young season.

The loss drops Colorado to 2-1 on the season after a strong start that included an 8-4 win over the Los Angeles Kings in the opener. The Avalanche had been riding momentum from Nathan MacKinnon's two-goal, one-fight performance earlier in the week.

The result is the first road setback of the year for Colorado, which continues a stretch of early-season games away from Ball Arena.

stories.headline: Denver names 26-member working group to develop data center regulations
stories.summary:
Mayor Mike Johnston and three Denver City Council members announced Wednesday the formation of a 26-person working group charged with developing policy recommendations for regulating data centers in the city. The group was selected from more than 250 applicants and includes representatives from utilities, academia, healthcare, air quality and community organizations, among them Ean Thomas Tafoya of GreenLatinos, former Colorado House Speaker Rev. Terrance Carroll and Xcel Energy's Melissa Almond.

The move comes as public concerns grow over data centers' demands on electricity, water and neighborhood character. The Denver metro area currently hosts 54 data centers, and the rapid expansion of such facilities nationally has intensified debate over where they should be permitted and under what conditions.

Johnston framed the effort as a matter of local control, saying Denver — not corporations — will decide if and how data centers may operate in the city. The group's first meeting is expected Friday, with sessions streamed in English and Spanish and public comment invited.

stories.headline: 10th Circuit overturns convictions in toddler exorcism death case tied to New Mexico compound near Colorado border
stories.summary:
A federal appeals court panel in Denver this week reversed the kidnapping convictions of two women and vacated terrorism and conspiracy convictions of two men stemming from the 2017 death of a 3-year-old boy during an exorcism at a remote compound in Amalia, New Mexico, just south of the Colorado state line. The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found insufficient evidence supported the kidnapping convictions against Hujrah Wahhaj and Subhanah Wahhaj and that a judge gave inaccurate jury instructions; neither woman can be retried on those charges.

The court also vacated terrorism and conspiracy-to-kill-federal-officers convictions against Lucas Morton and Siraj Wahhaj — the toddler's father — finding the two men, who represented themselves at trial, were wrongly excluded from bench conferences. Their cases may be retried. All four had been sentenced to life in prison in 2024.

The case centered on Siraj Wahhaj and spiritual leader Jany Leveille, who performed hours-long Muslim exorcism rituals on Abdul Ghani Wahhaj, believing the boy was afflicted by evil spirits. The child died on Dec. 24, 2017, and his body was stored in a tunnel on the compound property. The group had also been training with firearms at the compound, according to court records.

stories.headline: Broncos prepare for Week 5 matchup with Chargers after injury updates, offensive struggles
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos began preparations Wednesday for a Week 5 home game against the Los Angeles Chargers, who enter the matchup at 0-4. The team held media availability as coaches and players addressed the club's 2-2 start and ongoing questions about the offense under coordinator Davis Webb.

The Broncos are coming off a 24-14 loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Week 4, a game in which cornerback Pat Surtain II, receiver Courtland Sutton, and running back Jaleel McLaughlin exited with injuries. Team officials had indicated those injuries were not considered serious, and the club appears to be heading into the week with most of its key contributors available.

Denver's offense has struggled to find consistency through the first quarter of the season, generating scrutiny of Webb's play-calling and scheme. The Chargers matchup presents an opportunity for the Broncos to return to .500 with a win over one of the AFC's most struggling teams.

stories.headline: ESPN analysis: Nuggets' Watson trade signals ownership not fully committed to championship contention
stories.summary:
An ESPN roster analysis published this week identified Denver's decision to trade forward Peyton Watson to the Cleveland Cavaliers in an August sign-and-trade as the biggest hole on the Nuggets' roster heading into the season. The piece described Watson as an energetic 24-year-old capable of defending multiple positions and shooting 41 percent from three-point range — exactly the type of complementary player the capped-out Nuggets need.

The analysis concluded that Denver's move to prioritize cost-cutting over retaining Watson signaled that ownership was not fully committed to competing for a championship. The Nuggets lost their preseason opener 109-97 to the Utah Jazz, with forward Spencer Jones sidelined by a hamstring strain.

Denver enters the season with its core of Nikola Jokic, Jamal Murray and Michael Porter Jr. intact but with reduced depth around them. The Watson departure has drawn scrutiny as the team seeks to remain a Western Conference title contender.

stories.headline: Walmart and Wing to expand drone delivery service to Denver metro in 2027
stories.summary:
Walmart and Alphabet-owned Wing announced plans to expand their drone delivery service to the Denver metropolitan area next year, according to a Fox Business report. Denver would join Seattle as one of the next markets in the program's national rollout.

The expansion reflects growing retailer investment in last-mile delivery technology as competition for rapid fulfillment intensifies. Wing has operated drone delivery in limited U.S. markets and the addition of a large metro area like Denver would represent a significant scale-up of the service.

Details on which specific Denver-area Walmart locations would participate in the program and the timeline for launch have not yet been announced.

stories.headline: Denver police investigate early morning pedestrian crash on South Sheridan Boulevard
stories.summary:
Denver police are investigating a crash involving a pedestrian that occurred around 2:30 a.m. Wednesday near West Florida Avenue and South Sheridan Boulevard. One man was transported to a hospital with serious injuries following the incident.

Northbound lanes of South Sheridan Boulevard were closed during the police investigation. No additional details about the circumstances of the crash or the identities of those involved had been released as of Wednesday.

The incident is under active investigation by Denver Police.

stories.headline: Premier League Mornings Live fan festival coming to Denver's Union Station this weekend
stories.summary:
Premier League Mornings Live will set up at Denver's Union Station on Saturday and Sunday, bringing two days of free fan festivities to downtown Denver. The event will feature live broadcasts of Premier League matches in Mountain Time, meet-and-greet opportunities, appearances by legendary players and exclusive merchandise.

Three-time Premier League champion Ashley Cole is among the former players slated to appear. The festival is the 13th edition of the traveling event, which has drawn more than 120,000 attendees since its 2017 launch across cities including Los Angeles, Chicago, New York and Miami Beach.

Attendees are encouraged to use light rail or bus, as Union Station does not have a dedicated parking lot. A strict clear-bag policy is in effect, with bags limited to 12 inches by 6 inches by 12 inches.

stories.headline: Pokémon Fossil Museum exhibition to open at Denver Museum of Nature and Science in May 2027
stories.summary:
The Denver Museum of Nature and Science announced it will host the Pokémon Fossil Museum Exhibition beginning May 28, 2027. The exhibition blends actual fossil specimens with Pokémon themes, drawing connections between prehistoric creatures and the popular franchise's fictional fossil Pokémon.

The traveling exhibition has drawn large crowds internationally and represents a crossover between science education and pop culture. Denver's booking continues a trend of the museum hosting high-profile touring exhibitions to attract broader audiences.

Further details on ticketing and programming for the exhibition are expected to be released closer to the opening date.

stories.headline: October heat wave continues across Colorado with highs in the mid-80s through the weekend
stories.summary:
Unseasonably warm weather is persisting across Colorado, with Denver forecast to reach the mid-80s Thursday — approaching the October 8 record high of 85 degrees set in 2020. Temperatures are running 10 to 15 degrees above normal for this time of year, with overnight lows remaining in the low-to-mid 50s around the metro area.

Conditions are expected to remain mostly sunny and dry through Saturday, with limited rain chances confined mainly to the mountains. Winds will pick up Friday night and Saturday, with gusts up to 40 mph possible along the northern Front Range and in North Park.

A more meaningful pattern change is possible in the middle to latter part of next week as a storm system moves through the Pacific Northwest. Forecasters say cooler temperatures and improved rain chances could arrive in Denver by late next week, though the timing remains uncertain.

stories.headline: Mother Other vegan restaurant brings permanent home and seasonal menu to South Broadway
stories.summary:
Mother Other, a plant-based restaurant at 675 S. Broadway in Denver, opened this summer as the brick-and-mortar evolution of the Easy Vegan pop-up founded by Alexi Mandolini and Taylor Herbert during the COVID-19 pandemic. The couple built a following through appearances at South Pearl and City Park farmers markets and a winning run on Food Network's The Great Food Truck Race in 2023.

The restaurant updated its menu this week for the fall season, swapping summer offerings for dishes including an apple-and-kuri squash bisque and a French onion-and-sunchoke pierogi. A Japanese sweet potato dish — baked and topped with truffled taro chips, a tempura onion ring, miso-and-black-garlic whipped potato and Szechuan sesame chili oil — has remained on the menu since the beginning and is credited by Herbert as putting the business on the map.

Mandolini and Herbert said they deliberately avoided outside investors to maintain creative and business control. Customers from their farmers market days helped build out the new dining room, contributing tools and installing fixtures.

topStory.headline: Democrats Eye Red-State Senate Seats but Lack Funds to Compete Across Expanded Map
topStory.summary:
Democratic Senate candidates and outside groups are reporting competitive polling in deeply Republican states including Mississippi, Florida, South Carolina, Kansas and Texas, sparking debate within the party over whether to invest significantly beyond its traditional battleground states in the final weeks of the midterm election cycle. Party strategists and campaign committees acknowledge they do not have sufficient funds to both defend core competitive seats and make major financial plays in states that have long been considered out of reach.

American Bridge PAC announced Wednesday it is deploying $22.7 million across roughly 80 House and Senate races, including $2.1 million in Mississippi, $2.5 million in Florida, $630,000 in South Carolina and $410,000 in Kansas, primarily through billboard advertising targeting rising costs and economic hardship. American Bridge 21st Century President Pat Dennis said the investments reflect a long-term strategy to build a durable Democratic majority in new territory, while acknowledging such shifts do not happen in a single election cycle.

Mississippi Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom called on national party organizations to direct more resources to his state, arguing that voters there have been squeezed particularly hard by high gas prices and that the cost of advertising in Mississippi is relatively low. He contended that competitive polling demonstrates Democrats can win if they can get their message out, and accused the national party of historically ignoring the state.

Democrats are already spending in several states President Donald Trump carried by double-digit margins in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, stretching available resources further. A senior Democratic operative working on Senate races, speaking anonymously to discuss internal strategy, said national committees are in a belt-tightening posture and that funds are insufficient to simultaneously protect must-win seats and chase the next ring of competitive opportunities.

The tension reflects a recurring dilemma for the party: competitive polling in unexpected states generates pressure to invest, but past cycles have demonstrated that strong numbers do not always translate into wins when financial resources are spread thin. The decisions made in the coming weeks will determine whether Democrats pursue a narrow path to a Senate majority or gamble on a broader map with uncertain returns.
